sub_units.name: Number Systems
sub_units.content: Number Systems form the foundation of quantitative aptitude. This topic covers natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational and irrational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers. It also includes concepts like divisibility rules, prime numbers, factors, multiples, and properties of numbers. Mastering number systems is essential for solving a wide range of aptitude problems efficiently.

sub_units.name: HCF & LCM
sub_units.content: HCF (Highest Common Factor) and LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) are fundamental concepts used to find common divisors and multiples of numbers. HCF is the largest number that divides two or more numbers exactly, while LCM is the smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers. These concepts are widely applied in problems involving fractions, time intervals, and real-life scenarios like scheduling and distribution.

sub_units.name: Percentages
sub_units.content: Percentages represent a fraction out of 100 and are used extensively in daily life and competitive exams. This topic covers conversion between fractions, decimals, and percentages, percentage increase and decrease, successive percentage changes, and comparison using percentages. A strong understanding of percentages is the foundation for topics like Profit & Loss, Simple & Compound Interest, and Data Interpretation.

sub_units.name: Profit & Loss
sub_units.content: Profit and Loss is a practical application of percentages in business and trade scenarios. This topic covers cost price, selling price, marked price, discount, profit percentage, loss percentage, and successive discounts. Understanding these concepts helps solve problems related to buying, selling, and trade transactions commonly asked in aptitude tests.

sub_units.name: Ratio & Proportion
sub_units.content: Ratio is a way of comparing two or more quantities, while proportion states that two ratios are equal. This topic includes simplification of ratios, compound ratios, direct and inverse proportion, and problems involving distribution and mixing. Ratio and proportion form the basis for many advanced aptitude topics like mixtures, partnerships, and time-work problems.

sub_units.name: Averages
sub_units.content: Averages refer to the central value of a set of numbers, calculated by dividing the sum of all values by the count of values. This topic covers simple averages, weighted averages, average speed, and problems involving changes in averages when elements are added or removed. Averages are frequently tested in aptitude exams and form the basis for data interpretation questions.

sub_units.name: Simple & Compound Interest
sub_units.content: Simple Interest (SI) is calculated on the original principal amount, while Compound Interest (CI) is calculated on the principal plus accumulated interest. This topic covers formulas for SI and CI, difference between SI and CI, half-yearly and quarterly compounding, and real-life applications in banking and finance. These concepts are essential for both aptitude exams and financial literacy.

sub_units.name: Time & Work
sub_units.content: Time and Work problems involve calculating the time taken by individuals or groups to complete a task. This topic covers work done per unit time, combined work, efficiency-based problems, pipes and cisterns, and alternate working days. Understanding the relationship between time, work, and efficiency is crucial for solving these frequently asked aptitude questions.

sub_units.name: Time, Speed & Distance
sub_units.content: Time, Speed, and Distance problems are based on the fundamental relationship: Distance = Speed × Time. This topic covers average speed, relative speed, problems on trains, boats and streams, races, and circular track problems. These concepts are widely tested in aptitude exams and require a good understanding of unit conversions and proportional reasoning.

sub_units.name: Mixtures & Allegations
sub_units.content: Mixtures and Allegations deal with combining two or more ingredients at different prices or concentrations to form a mixture. The allegation method provides a quick way to find the ratio in which two ingredients should be mixed to get a desired average price or concentration. This topic is useful in solving problems related to solutions, alloys, and blended products commonly seen in aptitude exams.
